Case Study: Product & UX Design

Reps don't fear being coached. They fear being watched.

A five-day sprint redesigning COACH AI's rep onboarding, turning a surveillance tool into a silent partner reps actually trust, before they ever reach the dashboard.

Role: Product & UX Design, Solo Format: 5-Day Sprint Focus: Rep Onboarding
01 · The Problem

The gap isn't skill. It's trust.

COACH AI runs on trust between reps and supervisors, and that trust breaks down long before a rep ever opens the dashboard. Fixing the onboarding process closes that gap directly: it improves the quality of every recorded customer interaction, and it strengthens the KPI picture admins rely on, person to person.

Five psychological friction points recur across COACH AI's flow, and most of its competitors':

  • SuspiciousSTEP 1 · Tool Introduction & Onboarding

    Reps fear "big brother" surveillance and management micromanagement rather than seeing a supportive coaching tool.

  • InsecureSTEP 2 · Arrival at the Customer's Doorstep

    Reps feel self-conscious disclosing recording to prospects, leading them to delay recording or hide phones in pockets.

  • SkepticalSTEP 5 · AI Processing & Transcript Generation

    Users distrust AI outputs due to speaker misattributions, transcript errors, and unexplained black-box scores.

  • ImpatientSTEPS 3, 4, 6 · Capture, Session Management, Review

    Reps are frustrated by battery drain, lockouts from self-serve editing/trimming, missing transcript search, and overwhelming feedback.

  • RigidSTEPS 2, 6 · Doorstep, Manager Review

    Software enforces unyielding workflows: defaulting admins into ride-along views over analytics, with no state-aware consent assistance.

02 · The Landscape

A crowded category, one open lane

Before any of this got designed, the market got mapped: two funded incumbents, three fast-followers, and a field rep who still doesn't trust the app on his belt. That last part is the opening.

~$70M
Rilla's estimated ARR, up from $24M in 2024
$75M
Raised by Siro, now built into ServiceTitan Field Pro
5
Direct competitors launched or funded since 2025
$0
Coach's public pricing or named customers, the proof gap

Four rings of distance from Coach's own offering:

  • DirectRilla · Siro · SalesAsk · Craft · FrontlineIQ

    Same product, same customer: in-person AI coaching apps competing head-on. Rilla leads with 2,000+ accounts including Kohler and The Home Depot; Siro's distribution runs through ServiceTitan itself.

  • IndirectGong · Chorus · Mindtickle / Allego / Highspot

    Same underlying problem, built for office selling: conversation intelligence and enablement suites with no in-person field capture. Gong alone serves 4,500+ customers.

  • SubstituteManual ride-alongs · CRM recording · Pasting into ChatGPT

    What reps already do instead of buying software. Free, unscalable, and exactly the habits an onboarding flow has to displace.

  • EmergingServiceTitan Field Pro · Othello · Hyperbound · Second Nature

    New entrants and platform incumbents that could dominate next, plus the foundation model labs themselves lowering the cost of building this category's core feature.

AdvantageRep-first UX

Coaching framed around the rep's growth, not manager surveillance, fixes the category's number-one adoption killer. It's the same insight this entire sprint is built on.

AdvantageLate-mover clarity

Coach can copy the incumbents' proven playbooks and undercut them on price and transparency, the two things neither Rilla nor Siro currently publishes.

DisadvantageTiny and very late

An estimated ~$500K ARR against Rilla's ~$70M and Siro's $75M raised. No published pricing, no named customers, against rivals' marquee logos.

01
Undercut on transparency

Publish sub-$150 per user, per month pricing. Beat Rilla and Siro on price clarity and coaching latency.

02
Win a defensible vertical

Concentrate where incumbents are weakest, retail, door-to-door, or France, before expanding further.

03
Publish proof, fast

Convert the claimed 32% conversion lift into two or three named, verifiable case studies with real logos.

Move 01 is a pricing decision. Move 03 is a sales decision. What's actually underneath both of them is the one thing no competitor has designed for yet: the rep's own trust.

03 · The Approach

The Silent Partner

Five traits, five deliberate counter-moves. The onboarding dismantles each objection step by step, before the rep ever reaches the dashboard.

Suspicious →Steps 1–4

Warm Welcome reframes the tool from a manager's surveillance camera into a personal assistant: "Focus on your customer. We'll handle the notes." Then Rep Discovery asks the rep for their own strengths, weaknesses, and personality first, signaling: I work for you, and I'm tailoring my advice to your style. That destroys the feeling of a top-down mandate.

Insecure →Steps 5–6

Pocket Reality validates the instinct to hide the phone by turning it into an official feature. It's supposed to be tucked away. Comfortable Consent then hands reps the exact empathetic, low-pressure script they need, removing the social anxiety of disclosure.

Skeptical →Step 7

Transparency Promise meets this objection head-on, before a rep ever sees a bad score, promising "game film, fully transparent," and surfacing the Edit control during onboarding itself, not after trust has already broken.

Impatient →Step 8

One Small Win explicitly promises no 40-point checklist: just one friendly tip a day, lowering cognitive load and making the app feel calming rather than demanding.

Rigid →Steps 2–4

Rep Discovery is the real antidote to rigidity: a Relationship Builder gets entirely different feedback than a High-Performing Closer. The software flexes to match the human, instead of forcing the human into its playbook.

04 · Direction

Finding the palette

Early moodboarding centered on one working principle:

"Maximizing realism with human-centered personality."

That principle held, even as the palette itself moved, settling into a warm, low-glare cream paired with a deep forest green for focus states, and a single terracotta accent reserved for the moments that need it: recording, action, momentum.

07 · Process

Five days, thirteen hours

No stakeholder team, no design-by-committee: one pain point, chosen and pursued in public, on the clock.

DayHoursOutput
Day 12hLock one pain point. Pull competitor screenshots + 3–4 real user quotes. Zero design.
Day 23hWireframe one dashboard screen. Structure only.
Day 33hVisual pass on that screen + one launch asset. Type, color, one component.
Day 43hBuild the Figma Slides deck. 8 slides.
Day 52hPolish, 90-second Loom walkthrough, application note.

13 hours total, across 5 days.

08 · Closing

COACH AI does need a redesign. But more importantly, it needed permission, earned one screen at a time, before the rep ever presses record.
